extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and advanced creative writers studying narratology and narrative technique (e.g., analysis of Proust)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic guidance on how temporal displacements (analepses, prolepses), iterative/achronic structures, and ordering principles function in narrative and how to employ or recognize them in fiction. Focuses on classifying types, signals, effects on reader expectation, and organizational principles (geographic/thematic grouping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external prolepses (and heterodiegetic vs homodiegetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish internal prolepses (those within the narrator's diegesis) from external ones; heterodiegetic prolepses pose no risk of interference or duplication, while homodiegetic prolepses may.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal prolepses present the problem of interference/possible useless duplication between the first narrative and the proleptic section; thus they require attention to avoid redundancy. The text disregards heterodiegetic prolepses for which duplication risk is nil. Examples: various Proustian anticipations discussed in the Recherche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing prolepses (prolepses that fill a later blank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses that 'fill in ahead of time a later blank' by supplying information that later avoids an ellipsis or paralipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include quick evocations that offset future ellipses: Marcel's future years in school (Combray), the last scene between his father and Legrandin, the sequel of Swann-Odette erotic relations, anticipatory descriptions of the sea at Balbec, and notices of repeated dinners. Their function is to complete forthcoming lacunae in narrative by early disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeating prolepses (advance notices that double a section to come)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses that anticipate and slightly double a narrative section that will be told in full later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeating prolepses scarcely occur except as brief allusions and use canonical formulas like 'we will see' or 'one will see later.' They serve as advance notices, preparing the reader for forthcoming material without replacing it. Paradigm: the advance notice about the Montjouvain sacrilege scene in Proust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative prolepses (anticipating an entire series from the first instance)
rubrics_metrics.description: On encountering a 'first time' event, the narrative envisages in advance the whole series of occurrences that the first event inaugurates, treating the first as a paradigm of subsequent repetitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical for initiation scenes (first kiss, first sight of sea, first dinners), iterative prolepses open a view onto later series and make clear the paradigmatic function of the inaugural scene. They often register nostalgia for the 'primultimateness' of the first time and are frequent in Proust's big scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice vs advance mention
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance notices are explicit anticipations that create expectation and may resolve later; advance mentions are simple markers or allusive references whose significance is recognized only retrospectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance notice: explicitly anticipates (e.g., scene at Montjouvain), often signaled and meant to prepare interpretation. Advance mention: an 'insignificant seed' (e.g., early minor appearances or offhand references) that only later acquires importance. The reader's competence affects detection; authors may exploit false advance mentions as snares (detective-story technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader competence and the use of false advance mentions (narrative snares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can rely on readers' growing competence to detect 'seeds' and can deliberately offer false advance mentions (snares) to mislead or play with expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As readers acquire the ability to decode narrative codes, the author may include false snares; once the reader outmaneuvers these, the author may escalate to more sophisticated false snares. This is part of Proustian believability and the 'logic of inconsistency'—manipulating frustrated expectations and surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks/signals of prolepsis and return (explicit textual formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain verbal formulas explicitly mark the start and end of prolepses and indicate returns to the original narrative line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of proleptic marks: 'to anticipate for a moment', 'interrupting for a few moments our narrative', 'I take a leap of many years'; examples of return marks: 'To return to this first evening...', 'it is time to rejoin the Baron...', 'But I must return to my narrative...' Authors do not always avoid explicitness; such markers shape reader orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial vs complete prolepses (extent of anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses may be partial—often abruptly interrupted—or complete, where the anticipation continues up to the denouement (internal) or narrating moment (external).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author finds hardly any complete prolepses; most are partial and interrupted. Completeness is rare and is judged relative to story-denouement or narrating moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex anachronies (second- and third-degree effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anachronies can be layered (e.g., prolepsis on analepsis, analepsis on prolepsis), creating second- or third-degree temporal effects that complicate linear chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: anticipation of Swann's death on anticipation of his luncheon with Bloch; retrospection of Françoise on that same anticipation. Such nested movements speed up temporal seesaws and produce intricate narrative frequency and perspective effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double anachronies and inversion of textual/story order
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple anachronies occur, one can invert the relation between the textual order (order in which events appear in the text) and the story's chronological order, producing sentences like 'It would happen later, as we have already seen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analeptic status of whole sections (e.g., Un amour de Swann) can make an anticipation into a recall for the reader and vice versa; differentiating direction (later vs earlier) becomes delicate in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achrony (dateless/atemporal events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events attached only to commentarial discourse without temporal anchoring are dateless and ageless—achronies—because they are not linked to other events by earlier/later relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: anecdotes in Guermantes dinner or illustrative anecdotes (drawing master who never saw his mistress's hair color). Such events cannot be located temporally and illustrate narrative capacity to disengage arrangement from chronological dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/thematic syllepsis (ordering by kinship rather than chronology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative grouping can be governed by spatial (geographic syllepsis) or thematic kinship (thematic syllepsis) instead of chronological sequence, producing an order of succession based on sites or themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Transatlantic itinerary whose station order evokes anecdotes tied to stopping places; the closing pages of Combray where narrative order follows opposition Meseglise way/Guermantes way and spatial proximity rather than temporal sequence. Such grouping yields narrative autonomy from chronological order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective synthetic character / narrator omnitemporality
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator may hold simultaneously the whole work's threads, apprehending all moments and places together and establishing telescopic relationships among them—an 'omnitemporality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust's narrator, after his trance of unifying significance, continuously perceives the unity of his story and can juxtapose distant moments; this retrospective synthesis underpins frequent anachronies and atemporal commentarial discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distortions of speed as temporal devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating narrative speed (accelerations, retardations) contributes to emancipation from chronological temporality and functions alongside order-transgressions to shape narrative time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although treated in the next chapter, the page signals that distortions of speed are as important as chronological transgressions for achieving temporal autonomy in narrative; authors should consider speed alongside anachrony when shaping temporal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepses' function in reducing apparent adventitiousness (long-distance advance notices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-reach advance notices can provide provisional justification for episodes whose presence might otherwise seem gratuitous in separately published volumes, promoting work-wide cohesiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust used long-distance advance notices (e.g., references to future scenes or characters like Cottard or Verdurin dinners) to signal distant symmetry and architectural cohesion across volumes, reducing misunderstanding of seemingly episodic passages.
